new_note: *Fear Yahuah (God), and honor the priest; and give him his portion, as it is commanded you; the firstfruits, and the trespass offering, and the gift of the shoulders, and the sacrifice of sanctification, and the firstfruits of the holy things.* (Ecclesiasticus 7:31). *Honour Yahuah (LORD) with thy substance, and with the firstfruits of all thine increase:* (Proverbs 3:9). Sirach puts the priest's portion under the fear of Yahuah (God) and says it is given as it is commanded — the firstfruits, the trespass offering, the shoulder, the holy things. Solomon had already said where that honor is going: the firstfruits of all the increase honor Yahuah (LORD) himself, and the priest is the hand that receives them for him. Neither verse treats the gift as a tax. It is the first and the best handed back to the one who gave the whole, and the Torah's instruction for the priest's due is where that honor lands in practice.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 7:31 — *give him his portion, as it is commanded you; the firstfruits.* The firstfruits that honor Yahuah (LORD) in Proverbs 3:9 reach him through the priest's hand.

new_note: *And stretch yours hand to the poor, that your blessing may be perfected.* (Ecclesiasticus 7:32). *Naked, and ye clothed me: I was sick, and ye visited me: I was in prison, and ye came unto me.* (Matthew 25:36). Sirach says the hand stretched to the poor is what perfects the blessing — the blessing is not finished until it has gone out the door to someone in need. Yahusha (Jesus) sets the same thing as the measure at his judgment seat: the naked clothed, the sick visited, the prisoner visited, and he counts it as done to himself. Sirach keeps going in the next verses — be with them that weep, be not slow to visit the sick — and the list reads like the King's own. This is the fruit of the new heart Ezekiel promised, a heart that keeps his judgments because it has been made able to; a confession that never stretches out its hand has not yet been perfected into a blessing.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 7:32 — *stretch yours hand to the poor, that your blessing may be perfected.* The hand stretched to the poor is the measure the King uses at Matthew 25:36.

new_note: *Turn away your eye from a beautiful woman, and look not upon another’s beauty; for many have been deceived by the beauty of a woman; for herewith love is kindled as a fire.* (Ecclesiasticus 9:8). *But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart.* (Matthew 5:28). Sirach tells the eye to turn away before love is kindled as a fire, because the deception begins in the looking. Yahusha (Jesus) follows the same line to its root: the look that lusts has already committed the adultery in the heart. Neither is adding a new commandment to the seventh. Both are reading it where it was always meant to be read, at the eye and the heart, before the body ever moves.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 9:8 — *Turn away your eye from a beautiful woman.* The eye turned away in Sirach is the heart Yahusha (Jesus) reads at Matthew 5:28.

new_note: *Forsake not an old friend; for the new is not comparable to him: a new friend is as new wine; when it is old, you shall drink it with pleasure.* (Ecclesiasticus 9:10). *Neither do men put new wine into old bottles: else the bottles break, and the wine runneth out, and the bottles perish: but they put new wine into new bottles, and both are preserved.* (Matthew 9:17). Sirach honors the old friend and the old wine; the new has to age before it is worth drinking. Yahusha (Jesus) is not quarreling with that. The question put to him in Matthew 9 was about fasting, and his answer is about the vessel: new wine poured into a brittle old skin bursts it and both are lost. The Torah is neither the wine nor the skin; it is the vineyard the wine comes from. The skin that cannot stretch is the body of added tradition, and the wine the King pours will itself grow old and be drunk with pleasure, exactly as Sirach says new wine does.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 9:10 — *a new friend is as new wine; when it is old, you shall drink it with pleasure.* Sirach's new wine that ages well sits beside the new wine and new bottles of Matthew 9:17.
flag: Theology correction: the old note read Sirach's old-friend loyalty as itself the Pharisaic old wineskin that bursts — pitting the wisdom book against the gospel. Rewritten so the two agree: the Torah is neither wine nor skin, the brittle skin is added tradition, and Sirach's own line (new wine ages into pleasure) supports rather than opposes the King.

new_note: *As near as you can, guess at your neighbour, and consult with the wise.* (Ecclesiasticus 9:14). *He that walketh with wise men shall be wise: but a companion of fools shall be destroyed.* (Proverbs 13:20). Sirach says to take the measure of your neighbour as best you can and to take counsel from the wise, and in the next verse he says to let all your communication be in the law of the Most High. Solomon had said the same about company: walk with the wise and you grow wise, keep company with fools and you share their ruin. Who sits at your table shapes who you become.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 9:14 — *guess at your neighbour, and consult with the wise.* Sirach's consult with the wise is Solomon's walk with wise men at Proverbs 13:20.

new_note: *Let your talk be with the wise, and all your communication in the law of the Most High.* (Ecclesiasticus 9:15). *But his delight is in the law of Yahuah (LORD); and in his law doth he meditate day and night.* (Psalm 1:2). Sirach puts the whole of the wise man's conversation inside the law of the Most High. David's blessed man delights in the law of Yahuah (LORD) and meditates in it day and night. The one who delights in it will talk about it; the man whose speech is in the Torah is the man whose heart has been there first.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 9:15 — *all your communication in the law of the Most High.* Talk in the law of the Most High is the delight in the law of Psalm 1:2 spoken aloud.

new_note: *Pride is hateful before Yahuah (God) and man: and by both does one commit iniquity.* (Ecclesiasticus 10:7). *At the same time came the disciples unto Yahusha (Jesus), saying, Who is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven?* (Matthew 18:1). Sirach names pride as hateful before Yahuah (God) and man both, the root from which iniquity grows on either side. The disciples came to Yahusha (Jesus) asking who would be greatest in the kingdom; Mark records that they had been disputing it on the road. The question itself was the disposition Sirach warned against, and the King answered it by setting a child in their midst. The kingdom does not rank the way the kingdoms of the earth do.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 10:7 — *Pride is hateful before Yahuah (God) and man.* The pride Sirach names is the disposition behind who is the greatest at Matthew 18:1.

new_note: *The beginning of pride is when one departs from Yahuah (God), and his heart is turned away from his Maker.* (Ecclesiasticus 10:12). *And he said, Woe unto you also, ye lawyers! for ye lade men with burdens grievous to be borne, and ye yourselves touch not the burdens with one of your fingers.* (Luke 11:46). Sirach locates the beginning of pride in a heart turned away from its Maker. The lawyers Yahusha (Jesus) rebukes have built a weight of rules on top of the Torah and will not lift a finger under it themselves; the hand that adds to the commandment has already turned from the one who gave it. Voiding the commandment by addition is as much a departure as voiding it by subtraction, and both wear the robe of the law while they do it.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 10:12 — *The beginning of pride is when one departs from Yahuah (God).* The heart turned from its Maker is the lawyer lading burdens at Luke 11:46.

new_note: *For pride is the beginning of sin, and he that has it shall pour out abomination: and therefore Yahuah (God) brought upon them strange calamities, and overthrew them utterly.* (Ecclesiasticus 10:13). *Woe unto you, Pharisees! for ye love the uppermost seats in the synagogues, and greetings in the markets.* (Luke 11:43). Sirach traces sin to pride, and the overthrow of nations to the abomination pride pours out. The woe Yahusha (Jesus) pronounces falls on the love of the uppermost seats and the greetings in the markets — pride in a religious dress. The library had named the disease centuries before the Pharisee's table; the King names it at the table. The woe is on the man who loves the seat; the love of the uppermost place is the pride Sirach said sin begins in.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 10:13 — *pride is the beginning of sin, and he that has it shall pour out abomination.* The pride that begins sin is the love of the uppermost seats at Luke 11:43.

new_note: *For pride is the beginning of sin, and he that has it shall pour out abomination: and therefore Yahuah (God) brought upon them strange calamities, and overthrew them utterly.* (Ecclesiasticus 10:13). *Neither spared he the place where Lot sojourned, but abhorred them for their pride.* (Ecclesiasticus 16:8). Sirach's own proof case for pride comes later in his book: the place where Lot sojourned was not spared, and the reason he gives is their pride. The verse here says pride pours out abomination and brings strange calamities; the later verse names the city it happened to. Sodom is not a story about one sin. It is where pride ends when it is left to pour.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 10:13 — *Yahuah (God) brought upon them strange calamities, and overthrew them utterly.* The strange calamities of pride land on the place where Lot sojourned at Ecclesiasticus 16:8.

new_note: *Yahuah (God) has cast down the thrones of proud princes, and set up the meek in their stead.* (Ecclesiasticus 10:14). *Whosoever therefore shall humble himself as this little child, the same is greatest in the kingdom of heaven.* (Matthew 18:4). Sirach says Yahuah (God) has already done it: the proud cast off their thrones, the meek set in their place. Yahusha (Jesus) says the one who humbles himself as a little child is the greatest in the kingdom. It is the same hand moving in the same direction. The assembly is told to walk now by the measure the Father will judge by on that day.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 10:14 — *cast down the thrones of proud princes, and set up the meek in their stead.* The meek set up in the proud's stead is the child who is greatest at Matthew 18:4.

new_note: *Yahuah (God) has cast down the thrones of proud princes, and set up the meek in their stead.* (Ecclesiasticus 10:14). *And whosoever shall exalt himself shall be abased; and he that shall humble himself shall be exalted.* (Matthew 23:12). Sirach says the throne itself changes hands: the proud prince loses it and the meek receive it. Yahusha (Jesus) states the rule behind the history — exalt yourself and you are abased, humble yourself and you are exalted — and he says it in the middle of his rebuke of the scribes and Pharisees who loved the chief seats. This is not piety literature sitting beside the gospel; it is the same voice. What the Father does to kingdoms he does to men.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 10:14 — *cast down the thrones of proud princes, and set up the meek in their stead.* The thrones changing hands is the rule of Matthew 23:12 written as history.

new_note: *Prosperity and adversity, life and death, poverty and riches, come of Yahuah (God).* (Ecclesiasticus 11:14). *But seek ye first the kingdom of Elohim (God), and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you.* (Matthew 6:33). Sirach says both halves come from Yahuah (God) — prosperity and adversity, life and death, poverty and riches. That is the ground under Yahusha's (Jesus's) seek first: if the Father administers both, the citizen does not have to administer either, and can turn toward the kingdom and his righteousness with both hands. The adding comes from the same hand the adversity does.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 11:14 — *Prosperity and adversity, life and death, poverty and riches, come of Yahuah (God).* Because both come of Yahuah (God), the citizen can seek first the kingdom at Matthew 6:33.

new_note: *There is that waxeth rich by his wariness and pinching, and this is the portion of his reward:* (Ecclesiasticus 11:18). *But Elohim (God) said unto him, Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided?* (Luke 12:20). Sirach describes the man who grows rich by wariness and pinching and says, dryly, that this is the portion of his reward — the heap is all he gets. Yahusha (Jesus) gives the same man his night: the soul is required, and the goods pass to someone else. Hoarding is not a sin with no consequence. The consequence is that the hoard was the whole reward.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 11:18 — *waxeth rich by his wariness and pinching, and this is the portion of his reward.* The hoarder's whole reward is the heap left behind when the soul is required at Luke 12:20.

new_note: *Whereas he says, I have found rest, and now will eat continually of my goods; and yet he knoweth not what time shall come upon him, and that he must leave those things to others, and die.* (Ecclesiasticus 11:19). *And I will say to my soul, Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years; take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry.* (Luke 12:19). Sirach writes the rich fool's speech before the parable: I have found rest, I will eat continually of my goods. Yahusha (Jesus) puts nearly the same words in his mouth — take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry. Sirach had also named the two things the man never reckons with: he does not know what time is coming on him, and he must leave it all to others and die. The barns come down the same night.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 11:19 — *I have found rest, and now will eat continually of my goods.* Sirach's rich man speaks the rich fool's line of Luke 12:19 centuries early.

new_note: *Marvel not at the works of sinners; but trust in Yahuah (God), and abide in your labour: for it is an easy thing in the sight of Yahuah (God) on the sudden to make a poor man rich.* (Ecclesiasticus 11:21). *His lord said unto him, Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord.* (Matthew 25:21). Sirach tells the labourer not to marvel at how sinners get on, but to trust Yahuah (God) and stay at the work, because he can make a poor man rich in a moment. The faithful servant of the parable did exactly that — did not look sideways, did not stop, traded what he was given — and heard well done. The commendation is for the faithfulness, not the size of the return; the servant with two talents heard the same words as the one with five.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 11:21 — *trust in Yahuah (God), and abide in your labour.* Abiding in the labour is what earns well done, thou good and faithful servant at Matthew 25:21.

new_note: *For it is an easy thing to Yahuah (God) in the day of death to reward a man according to his ways.* (Ecclesiasticus 11:26). *Blessed is that servant, whom his lord when he cometh shall find so doing.* (Matthew 24:46). Sirach says the reward according to a man's ways is an easy thing for Yahuah (God) at the day of death. Yahusha (Jesus) blesses the servant found so doing when the lord returns — found at the work, not found having once begun it. The reward follows the ways walked through the whole delay. The day of death and the day of the lord's coming come to the same servant, and what he is found doing is the whole question.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 11:26 — *in the day of death to reward a man according to his ways.* Reward according to his ways is the servant found so doing at Matthew 24:46.

new_note: *Give to the godly man, and help not a sinner.* (Ecclesiasticus 12:4). *And it came to pass, as Yahusha (Jesus) sat at meat in the house, behold, many publicans and sinners came and sat down with him and his disciples.* (Matthew 9:10). Sirach says to give to the godly man and not to help a sinner, and the next verse shows what he means — bread given to the ungodly becomes strength he uses against you. Yahusha (Jesus) sat at meat with publicans and sinners. These are not two stances at war. The sinners at that table had come to him, and he was calling them to repentance, not feeding them in their sin. Sirach guards the hand; the King opens the door; and the Pharisee who turned the one into a wall against persons had misread it and could not see the other.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 12:4 — *Give to the godly man, and help not a sinner.* Sirach guards the hand from strengthening the ungodly; the King's table at Matthew 9:10 calls sinners to turn.
flag: Theology correction: the old note said Sirach 12 taught a wrong, categorical exclusion that the King reversed and superseded — pitting a scripture-level book against the gospel and dismissing Sirach's almsgiving counsel. Rewritten so both hold: Sirach warns against strengthening the ungodly in their wickedness with your bread; Yahusha (Jesus) eats with sinners who came to hear and are being called to repentance. The system that turned the caution into a wall around the table is what is corrected, not Sirach.

new_note: *Do well to him that is lowly, but give not to the ungodly: hold back your bread, and give it not to him, lest he overmaster you thereby: for else you shall receive twice as much evil for all the good you shall have done to him.* (Ecclesiasticus 12:5). *And when the Pharisees saw it, they said unto his disciples, Why eateth your Master with publicans and sinners?* (Matthew 9:11). Sirach says to do well to the lowly but to hold back your bread from the ungodly, because what you give him he will turn into power over you. The Pharisees asked why the Master ate with publicans and sinners, as if this verse had been broken. It had not. Sirach is warning against strengthening a man in his wickedness; Yahusha (Jesus) was eating with men who had come to hear him and were being called out of theirs. The ungodly in Sirach is the man who stays ungodly with your bread in his hand; the sinner at the King's table is the one who heard and sat down.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 12:5 — *hold back your bread, and give it not to him, lest he overmaster you thereby.* Bread held back from the one who would overmaster you is not the table the Pharisees question at Matthew 9:11.
flag: Theology correction: the old note said Sirach 12 taught a wrong, categorical exclusion that the King reversed and superseded — pitting a scripture-level book against the gospel and dismissing Sirach's almsgiving counsel. Rewritten so both hold: Sirach warns against strengthening the ungodly in their wickedness with your bread; Yahusha (Jesus) eats with sinners who came to hear and are being called to repentance. The system that turned the caution into a wall around the table is what is corrected, not Sirach.

new_note: *Give to the good, and help not the sinner.* (Ecclesiasticus 12:7). *But go ye and learn what that meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice: for I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.* (Matthew 9:13). Sirach says it again: give to the good, help not the sinner. Yahusha (Jesus) says he came not to call the righteous but sinners to repentance, and he sends the Pharisees to learn what mercy and not sacrifice means. The two verses meet at the word repentance. Sirach withholds help from the sinner who stays a sinner; the King calls the sinner to stop being one, and the mercy he names is the call itself. Neither verse feeds a man in his wickedness, and neither shuts the door on the man who turns.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 12:7 — *Give to the good, and help not the sinner.* Help not the sinner and call sinners to repentance (Matthew 9:13) meet at the word repentance.
flag: Theology correction: the old note said Sirach 12 taught a wrong, categorical exclusion that the King reversed and superseded — pitting a scripture-level book against the gospel and dismissing Sirach's almsgiving counsel. Rewritten so both hold: Sirach warns against strengthening the ungodly in their wickedness with your bread; Yahusha (Jesus) eats with sinners who came to hear and are being called to repentance. The system that turned the caution into a wall around the table is what is corrected, not Sirach.

new_note: *An enemy speaks sweetly with his lips, but in his heart he imagineth how to throw you into a pit: he will weep with his eyes, but if he find opportunity, he will not be satisfied with blood.* (Ecclesiasticus 12:16). *And forthwith he came to Yahusha (Jesus), and said, Hail, master; and kissed him.* (Matthew 26:49). Sirach draws the enemy who speaks sweetly with his lips while planning the pit, who weeps with his eyes and is not satisfied with blood. Judas came with Hail, master, and a kiss. The sweet lips and the pit were never far apart in the Hebrew library, and Yahusha (Jesus) knew the pattern before the kiss landed. The betrayer is the old enemy of the proverbs with a face.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 12:16 — *An enemy speaks sweetly with his lips, but in his heart he imagineth how to throw you into a pit.* The enemy with sweet lips is Judas with Hail, master, and a kiss at Matthew 26:49.

new_note: *The envious man has a wicked eye; he turns away his face, and despiseth men.* (Ecclesiasticus 14:8). *But if thine eye be evil, thy whole body shall be full of darkness. If therefore the light that is in thee be darkness, how great is that darkness!* (Matthew 6:23). Sirach calls envy a wicked eye and says the man who has it turns away his face and despises men. Yahusha (Jesus) says the evil eye fills the whole body with darkness. In the Hebrew idiom the evil eye is not a vague picture of bad vision; it is the stingy, envious heart that closes its hand and looks away. The King is speaking the idiom Sirach spoke, and the darkness he names is the darkness of the closed hand.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 14:8 — *The envious man has a wicked eye.* Sirach's wicked eye of envy is the evil eye that darkens the body at Matthew 6:23.

new_note: *A covetous man’s eye is not satisfied with his portion; and the iniquity of the wicked drieth up his soul.* (Ecclesiasticus 14:9). *But if thine eye be evil, thy whole body shall be full of darkness. If therefore the light that is in thee be darkness, how great is that darkness!* (Matthew 6:23). Sirach says the covetous eye is never satisfied with its portion, and that the iniquity dries the soul up. Yahusha (Jesus) says the evil eye leaves the whole body full of darkness. A dried-up soul and a darkened body are two ways of describing one man — the grasping one who never has enough and cannot see by his own light.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 14:9 — *A covetous man’s eye is not satisfied with his portion.* The unsatisfied eye that dries the soul is the evil eye of Matthew 6:23.

new_note: *A wicked eye envies his bread, and he is a niggard at his table.* (Ecclesiasticus 14:10). *But if thine eye be evil, thy whole body shall be full of darkness. If therefore the light that is in thee be darkness, how great is that darkness!* (Matthew 6:23). Sirach brings the wicked eye to the table: the host who begrudges his own bread even as he serves it. Yahusha (Jesus) asks how great the darkness is when the light itself has gone dark. Bread can cross a table with no blessing in it. The niggard's whole hospitality is darkness, however much he puts out, because the eye behind it is closed.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 14:10 — *A wicked eye envies his bread, and he is a niggard at his table.* The niggard's table is the darkness of Matthew 6:23 with bread on it.

new_note: *My son, according to your ability do good to thyself, and give Yahuah (God) his due offering.* (Ecclesiasticus 14:11). *And said, Naked came I out of my mother’s womb, and naked shall I return thither: Yahuah (LORD) gave, and Yahuah (LORD) hath taken away; blessed be the name of Yahuah (LORD).* (Job 1:21). Sirach says to do good to yourself as you are able and to give Yahuah (God) his due offering, and his very next line is the reason: death will not be long in coming. Job said at the ash heap what Sirach is building on — a man comes naked and goes back naked, and what he had in between was Yahuah's (God's) to give and to take. Everything in the hand is on loan. Give the Giver his due while it is still in your hand to give.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 14:11 — *according to your ability do good to thyself, and give Yahuah (God) his due offering.* Give Yahuah (God) his due while it is in your hand; Job 1:21 says who gave it and who takes it.

new_note: *Say not you, It is through Yahuah (God) that I fell away: for you oughtest not to do the things that he hates.* (Ecclesiasticus 15:11). *Not that which goeth into the mouth defileth a man; but that which cometh out of the mouth, this defileth a man.* (Matthew 15:11). Sirach forbids a man to say he fell away through Yahuah (God); the things he hates are not his doing. Yahusha (Jesus) says defilement does not come in through the mouth but out of it — the source is the man's own heart. The two verses fence off the same lie from opposite sides: the Father does not cause the falling, and bread eaten with unwashed hands does not cause the defilement. What a man does and says comes from inside him, and that is where the Torah has always located it.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 15:11 — *Say not you, It is through Yahuah (God) that I fell away.* The fall is not from Yahuah (God), and the defilement is not from the food (Matthew 15:11); both come from the man.

new_note: *For the wisdom of Yahuah (God) is great, and he is mighty in power, and beholds all things:* (Ecclesiasticus 15:18). *The eyes of Yahuah (LORD) are in every place, beholding the evil and the good.* (Proverbs 15:3). Sirach says the wisdom of Yahuah (God) beholds all things and his power is great. Solomon put the same truth in one line: his eyes are in every place, on the evil and the good alike. The verses before this in Sirach say life and death are set before a man and he will be given what he chooses; the all-seeing eye is why the choice is weighed and not forgotten.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 15:18 — *he is mighty in power, and beholds all things.* Sirach's all-beholding Yahuah (God) is the eyes in every place of Proverbs 15:3.

new_note: *He has commanded no man to do wickedly, neither has he given any man licence to sin.* (Ecclesiasticus 15:20). *But those things which proceed out of the mouth come forth from the heart; and they defile the man.* (Matthew 15:18). Sirach says plainly that Yahuah (God) has commanded no man to do wickedly and given no man licence to sin. Yahusha (Jesus) says what defiles a man comes out of his own heart. Put the two together and the source of sin is found — not the Father, not the bread, not the unwashed hands the Pharisees fussed over, but the heart. Any teaching that gives licence to sin is giving what Yahuah (God) never gave.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 15:20 — *He has commanded no man to do wickedly, neither has he given any man licence to sin.* No licence to sin from Yahuah (God); the sin comes out of the heart at Matthew 15:18.

new_note: *As his mercy is great, so is his correction also: he judges a man according to his works* (Ecclesiasticus 16:12). *For the Son of Adam shall come in the glory of his Father with his angels; and then he shall reward every man according to his works.* (Matthew 16:27). Sirach holds mercy and correction in the same hand and says the measure of both is a man's works. Yahusha (Jesus) says the same about his own coming in his Father's glory: every man rewarded according to his works. Grace is the door home, not the cancelling of the reckoning. The judgment weighs the fruit, and the fruit comes from a heart that either received the new heart Ezekiel promised or did not.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 16:12 — *he judges a man according to his works.* Judged according to his works is the Son of Adam's reward at Matthew 16:27.

new_note: *Make way for every work of mercy: for every man shall find according to his works.* (Ecclesiasticus 16:14). *For the Son of Adam shall come in the glory of his Father with his angels; and then he shall reward every man according to his works.* (Matthew 16:27). Sirach ties the two halves together: make way for every work of mercy, because every man shall find according to his works. Yahusha (Jesus) says the finding happens when the Son of Adam comes in his Father's glory. Mercy done now is what is found then. The door home is opened by grace; what is weighed at the judgment is what the one who came home did after he walked in.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 16:14 — *Make way for every work of mercy: for every man shall find according to his works.* Every man finds according to his works when the Son of Adam comes at Matthew 16:27.

new_note: *Make way for every work of mercy: for every man shall find according to his works.* (Ecclesiasticus 16:14). *Verily I say unto you, That he shall make him ruler over all his goods.* (Matthew 24:47). Sirach says every man shall find according to his works. The faithful and wise servant of Matthew 24 found more — ruler over all his goods — because he was found faithful with the household he had. The one-time confession that the pulpits treat as the whole account is not what either verse describes. The finding is according to the walking, and the servant is rewarded for what he was found doing through the long wait.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 16:14 — *every man shall find according to his works.* Finding according to works is the servant made ruler over all his goods at Matthew 24:47.

new_note: *He endued them with strength by themselves, and made them according to his image,* (Ecclesiasticus 17:3). *And he saith unto them, Whose is this image and superscription?* (Matthew 22:20). Sirach says the Maker made men according to his image, with strength of their own, carrying Genesis 1 forward. Yahusha (Jesus) held up the coin and asked whose image and superscription it bore. The coin bears Caesar's image and goes back to Caesar; the man bears the Father's image and belongs to the Father. The question about the tribute was a question about ownership, and Sirach had already said who stamped the man.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 17:3 — *made them according to his image.* The image stamped on man is the image the King asks about at Matthew 22:20.

new_note: *Beside this he gave them knowledge, and the law of life for an heritage.* (Ecclesiasticus 17:11). *And he said unto him, Why callest thou me good? there is none good but one, that is, Elohim (God): but if thou wilt enter into life, keep the commandments.* (Matthew 19:17). Sirach calls the law a law of life, given for an heritage along with knowledge. Yahusha (Jesus) tells the young man that if he would enter into life he should keep the commandments. The law of life and entering into life are the same road. Moses set life and good before Yashar'el (Israel) in the commandments, Sirach calls that inheritance by its name, and the King does not amend it when the question is put to him directly.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 17:11 — *the law of life for an heritage.* The law of life is the keep the commandments that enters into life at Matthew 19:17.

new_note: *Beside this he gave them knowledge, and the law of life for an heritage.* (Ecclesiasticus 17:11). *They say unto him, Cæsar’s. Then saith he unto them, Render therefore unto Cæsar the things which are Cæsar’s; and unto Elohim (God) the things that are Elohim's (God’s).* (Matthew 22:21). Sirach says the law of life was given as an heritage — set on the people along with the image. Yahusha (Jesus) says to render to Elohim (God) the things that are Elohim's (God's). What is Elohim's (God's) is what he put on the man: his image, and the law he gave for the man's inheritance. Rendering it back is not a burden laid on a free man; it is the heir keeping his inheritance.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 17:11 — *he gave them knowledge, and the law of life for an heritage.* The law of life given as heritage is among the things that are Elohim's (God's) at Matthew 22:21.

new_note: *And he said to them, Beware of all unrighteousness; and he gave every man commandment concerning his neighbour.* (Ecclesiasticus 17:14). *And the second is like unto it, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.* (Matthew 22:39). Sirach says the commandment concerning the neighbour was given to every man, in the same breath as the warning against all unrighteousness — this is Sinai, where their eyes saw his glory and their ears heard his voice. When Yahusha (Jesus) names the second great commandment he is quoting the Torah, the commandment Sirach is describing. The King added nothing. He put his finger on what was given at the beginning.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 17:14 — *he gave every man commandment concerning his neighbour.* The commandment concerning the neighbour is the second great commandment of Matthew 22:39.

new_note: *But to them that repent, he granted them return, and comforted those that failed in patience.* (Ecclesiasticus 17:24). *He answered and said, I will not: but afterward he repented, and went.* (Matthew 21:29). Sirach says Yahuah (God) grants return to them that repent and comforts those who failed in patience. The first son in the parable said I will not, then repented and went — and he is the one who did the father's will. The publicans and harlots Yahusha (Jesus) names a few lines later walked the same road: a no at first, and then a return. Return is granted to the one who turns, not to the one who said the right word and stayed where he was.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 17:24 — *to them that repent, he granted them return.* Return granted to them that repent is the son who afterward repented, and went at Matthew 21:29.

new_note: *But to them that repent, he granted them return, and comforted those that failed in patience.* (Ecclesiasticus 17:24). *For I have no pleasure in the death of him that dieth, saith Adonai Yahuah (the Lord GOD): wherefore turn yourselves, and live ye.* (Ezekiel 18:32). Sirach says return is granted to them that repent. Ezekiel heard the heart behind it: Adonai Yahuah (the Lord GOD) has no pleasure in the death of the one who dies, and so he calls, turn yourselves, and live. The granting of return is not reluctant. It is what he wanted all along.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 17:24 — *to them that repent, he granted them return, and comforted those that failed in patience.* Return granted to the penitent is the no pleasure in the death of him that dieth of Ezekiel 18:32.

new_note: *Return to Yahuah (God), and forsake your sins, make your prayer before his face, and offend less.* (Ecclesiasticus 17:25). *Draw nigh to Elohim (God), and he will draw nigh to you. Cleanse your hands, ye sinners; and purify your hearts, ye double minded.* (James 4:8). Sirach says to return, forsake sins, pray before his face, and offend less. James says to draw nigh to Elohim (God) and he will draw nigh to you, and he says it to sinners with unclean hands and double minds. Both put the turning first and the nearness after. The prayer before his face and the drawing nigh are one movement, and both expect the hands to be cleansed on the way.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 17:25 — *make your prayer before his face, and offend less.* Prayer before his face and offending less is James's draw nigh and cleanse your hands at James 4:8.

new_note: *Turn again to the Most High, and turn away from iniquity: for he will lead you out of darkness into the light of health, and hate you abomination vehemently.* (Ecclesiasticus 17:26). *Therefore I will judge you, O house of Yashar'el (Israel), every one according to his ways, saith Adonai Yahuah (the Lord GOD). Repent, and turn yourselves from all your transgressions; so iniquity shall not be your ruin.* (Ezekiel 18:30). Sirach says to turn again to the Most High and away from iniquity, and promises light at the end of it. Ezekiel says the same to the house of Yashar'el (Israel): repent, turn from your transgressions, so iniquity shall not be your ruin. The turn is what keeps iniquity from being the end of the story. Judgment according to a man's ways and the open call to turn stand in the same verse because they are the same mercy.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 17:26 — *Turn again to the Most High, and turn away from iniquity.* Turn away from iniquity is Ezekiel's so iniquity shall not be your ruin at Ezekiel 18:30.

new_note: *The number of a man’s days at the most are an hundred years.* (Ecclesiasticus 18:9). *As for man, his days are as grass: as a flower of the field, so he flourisheth.* (Psalm 103:15). Sirach puts the limit on a man's days at a hundred years at the most, and in the next verse calls a thousand years a drop of water to the sea beside eternity. David says man's days are as grass and he flourishes as a flower of the field. A hundred years and a flower's season are the same length against eternity, and both writers say it so the reader will spend them rightly.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 18:9 — *The number of a man’s days at the most are an hundred years.* A hundred years at the most is the flower of the field of Psalm 103:15.
